Strip Chart Recorder Working Principle: Pen and Thermal Head, Chart Speed, Zero and Span, Types and Troubleshooting

A paper recorder turns a 4 to 20 mA or thermocouple signal into a trace you can read across a time grid. The pen, the chart drive and the zero and span settings work together, and the time on the chart follows from the speed in mm/h.

Null balance servo Chart speed mm/h Zero and span Paperless recorders Calculator

A paper trend recorder writes a process value against time on a moving chart, and it is still found on furnaces, cold rooms and test benches. This guide covers how it works, the main types, how to read the chart and how to work out chart speed.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how a strip chart recorder works, how to set its chart speed, zero and span, and how to read and troubleshoot the trace.
Quick Answer

What is a strip chart recorder and how does it work?

Strip chart recorder is the name for an instrument that writes a process signal as a continuous trace on a paper strip moving at a fixed speed, so position across the chart gives the value and distance along it gives time. For example, at 20 mm/h with 5 mm divisions each division equals 15 minutes, and a pen sitting 65 mm across a 100 mm chart scaled 0 to 400 °C reads 260 °C.

What Is a Strip Chart Recorder?

A strip chart recorder is an instrument that draws a process variable such as temperature, pressure or flow on a long strip of paper moving under a pen at constant speed. The pen moves across the paper in proportion to the signal and the paper movement adds the time axis, so you get a permanent graph of value against time.

Key Facts
  • Inputs: 4 to 20 mA, 1 to 5 V, mV, thermocouple or RTD
  • Chart speed is set in mm/h, for example 20 mm/h
  • Time per division = division size ÷ chart speed
  • Types: galvanometric, potentiometric servo, thermal and paperless

You will find this recorder on panels near furnaces, in boiler rooms and in labs, often working next to a DCS historian rather than in place of it. The historian keeps years of data; the chart gives the local operator and the auditor a hard copy nobody can edit later.

Advertisement

How Does a Strip Chart Recorder Work?

A strip chart recorder works by moving a pen or print head across the chart in proportion to the input while a separate drive pulls the paper forward at a fixed speed. Together they draw value against time on the printed grid.

In the common null balance design the input is compared with a voltage from a slidewire, which is a potentiometer whose wiper moves with the pen. The difference is amplified and drives a servo motor until the two voltages match, and then the motor stops with the pen at the value.

The input usually comes from a transmitter on a 4 to 20 mA loop or straight from a thermocouple or RTD. In the diagram, 14.4 mA on a 0 to 400 °C range is 65% of span, so the pen settles 65 mm across a 100 mm chart and reads 260 °C.

1
Signal in
The input card takes mA, V, mV, thermocouple or RTD.
2
Compare
The error amplifier compares it with the slidewire voltage.
3
Drive the pen
The servo motor moves the pen carriage until the error is zero.
4
Move the paper
The chart drive pulls the paper at the set mm/h.
5
Mark the trace
A pen, dot printer or thermal head marks the chart.

Wikipedia explains that the chart drive is often a small synchronous motor locked to mains frequency, turning a gear train at constant speed. Newer units use a stepper motor under microprocessor control, which is how one recorder offers many speeds from a menu.

Quick Tip

If a trace is slow to follow a step change, check the input filter first. It behaves just like transmitter damping on the trace.

Chart Speed, Zero and Span Settings

Chart speed decides how much time each millimetre of paper holds, while zero and span decide which values sit on the left and right edges of the chart. If either is wrong, the trace still looks neat but the values on it are wrong.

The ABB SR100A data sheet lists chart speeds configurable in 1 mm steps from 1 to 1500 mm/h. A slow speed packs weeks onto one roll, while a fast speed spreads a short event so you can see its shape.

Chart speedTime per 10 mm25 m roll lastsTypical use
10 mm/h1 h2500 h (104.2 days)Slow tank or room trends
20 mm/h30 min1250 h (52.1 days)Cold store, utility logs
60 mm/h10 min416.7 h (17.4 days)Furnace or batch cycles
600 mm/h1 min41.7 h (1.7 days)Short tests, trip events

Zero is the value at the 0% line and span is the range from 0% to 100%, exactly as on a transmitter. With 0 to 400 °C on a 100 mm chart each millimetre is 4 °C, and a shift in either setting shows up as the zero and span errors you know from calibration.

Types of Paper and Paperless Recorders

The four types you will meet are galvanometric, potentiometric servo, thermal array and paperless (videographic) recorders. They differ in how the pen moves, how fast they respond and whether they use paper at all.

Galvanometric

A light moving coil in a magnet field carries the pen, like a meter pointer that writes.

Best for: Fast signals in labs
Fast
Potentiometric servo

Null balance loop with slidewire feedback drives the pen with a motor.

Best for: Process panels, furnaces
Accurate
Thermal array

A fixed thermal head with many dots heats special paper, with no moving pens.

Best for: Multichannel test logs
No ink
Paperless videographic

An ADC and microprocessor store data in memory and show the trend on a screen.

Best for: Pharma, food, new projects
Digital

Wikipedia notes that servo recorders handle a wide range of signals but respond slowly, so they suit signals that change over about a second or more. Galvanometric units are faster because the coil is light, the same idea used in a CRO where speed matters more than force.

A continuous recorder has one pen per channel and draws solid lines, while a multipoint recorder uses one print head that visits each channel in turn and prints a dot with a channel number. Engineers Edge describes these multichannel units as economical but slower than pen types.

Do You Know?

The ABB SR100A data sheet quotes a pen life of about 4 months, an update time of 800 ms for six traces and a resolution of 0.2% of span. It also gives one month of recording at 20 mm/h in a cold store example.

Advertisement

How to Read Strip Chart Paper

To read a strip chart recorder chart, take the pen position as a percentage of chart width, convert it with zero and span, and read the time from the line along the paper. On most panel units the newest trace sits next to the pen, so older data moves away in the direction of paper travel.

Value = Zero + (Pen position ÷ Width) × Span
Value = 0 + (65 ÷ 100) × 400
Value = 260 °C

Write the date, tag and chart speed on the paper when you load a new roll. Without that note nobody can be sure what a division means later.

Chart Speed and Time per Division Calculation

Time per division equals division size in millimetres divided by chart speed in mm/h, and chart duration equals chart length divided by the same speed. The infographic below shows the solved example.

Time per division t = d ÷ v
t = 5 mm ÷ 20 mm/h = 0.25 h
t = 15 min per division
Chart duration T = L ÷ v
T = 25000 mm ÷ 20 mm/h
T = 1250 h ≈ 52.1 days

The ABB SR100A takes a 25 m roll or a 12 m fanfold chart, so 20 mm/h gives 1250 h on the roll and 600 h on fanfold.

Chart Speed and Time per Division Calculator
Result
15 min per division, chart lasts 1250 h (52.1 days)

Turn the formula around to pick a speed. To spread a 2 minute event over 10 mm you need 10 ÷ (2 ÷ 60), which is 300 mm/h, while at 20 mm/h the same event fits in under 1 mm.

Quick Tip

When a temperature data logger replaces an old strip chart recorder, base the log interval on the old chart. At 20 mm/h a 0.5 mm pen line covers 1.5 minutes, so a 1 minute log is already finer.

Where Is a Paper Chart Recorder Still Used?

A strip chart recorder stays where a signed hard copy is wanted, where operators want a quick look at the trend on the panel, or where there is no computer at the machine. Wikipedia also mentions sites with no power and users who cannot view data on a computer.

Heat treatment furnaces
Multipoint charts kept with each batch record.
Cold stores
Long charts at slow speed for storage temperature.
Boiler panels
Steam pressure and drum level trends.
Autoclaves
Temperature and pressure for each load.

Furnace traces usually come from thermocouples and RTDs, and the recorder input card handles linearisation and cold junction compensation itself, which saves a transmitter per point.

Do You Know?

Engineers Edge notes that circular chart recorders rotate once in standard periods such as one hour, 24 hours or seven days, which suits batches of known length. Strip charts suit continuous processes.

Strip Chart Recorder vs Paperless Recorder Selection

Choose a paper strip chart recorder for a simple hard copy with few channels, and a paperless recorder when you need many channels, alarms, electronic records and network export. Most new projects in India now specify paperless units, while paper units remain common as replacements.

Paper recorder strengths
  • Instant trend without any software
  • Hard copy that cannot be edited later
  • Easy like for like panel replacement
Paper recorder limits
  • Pens and charts cost money every month
  • Few traces before the chart gets crowded
  • Data read by eye, not searched

Pharma and food sites supplying the US often ask for paperless units with audit trails and electronic signatures aimed at US FDA 21 CFR Part 11. On a plant network a paperless unit also feeds SCADA trending directly.

Compare input types, channels, chart width, speed range and accuracy from the data sheet, and weigh that accuracy against your loop using instrument accuracy and error basics. A 0.2% recorder on a 1% transmitter will not improve the reading.

Strip Chart Recorder Troubleshooting

Most faults on a strip chart recorder come from the input signal, the pen or print head, the chart drive or the paper. Work through them in that order, as the flowchart shows.

SymptomLikely causeCheck
Pen at 100% or 0%Open thermocouple, broken loopMeasure input at terminals
Noisy tracePoor shield or earth, VFD noiseShield earthed at one end
Trace offsetZero drift or wrong rangeInject 0% and 100%
Time scale wrongWrong speed, slipping driveMark paper, time 1 h
Pen huntsServo gain, dirty slidewireClean slidewire

A multifunction process calibrator lets you source 4, 12 and 20 mA and watch the pen settle at 0, 50 and 100%. Note the as found readings and use our calibration error calculator before you adjust anything.

Myth: A smooth trace means the reading is correct.
Fact: A wrong zero or span still draws a smooth line.
Myth: A faster chart speed makes the recorder more accurate.
Fact: Speed only spreads time; accuracy comes from the input.
Myth: Any chart paper of the right width will do.
Fact: Grid and perforations must match the model.
  • Chart speed setting matches the speed written on the paper
  • Zero and span match the printed scale and loop range
  • Pen has ink and the correct chart paper is loaded
  • Input checked at 0, 50 and 100% with a calibrator

Use these during recorder loop checks.

After a repair, run a full loop check from transmitter to recorder to prove the whole chain. Sign and date the chart at the test point so the record shows when it was verified.

Strip Chart Recorder FAQ

What is the difference between a galvanometric and a potentiometric recorder?

A galvanometric recorder moves the pen directly with a moving coil, so it is fast but has little pen force. A potentiometric recorder uses a servo motor and slidewire feedback, so it is slower, suiting signals that change over about a second, but more accurate.

How to calculate time per division on a chart recorder step by step?

Divide the division size in mm by the chart speed in mm/h to get hours, then multiply by 60 for minutes. For 5 mm divisions at 20 mm/h, 5 ÷ 20 is 0.25 h, which is 15 minutes per division.

How long will a 25 m chart roll last at 20 mm/h?

Divide chart length by chart speed, so 25000 mm ÷ 20 mm/h gives 1250 hours, or about 52.1 days. A 12 m fanfold chart at the same speed lasts 600 hours, which is 25 days, so keep spare charts ready before the month ends.

Why does my strip chart recorder pen go to full scale and stay there?

The most common cause is an open thermocouple or a broken input loop with upscale burnout selected in the recorder. Measure the signal at the recorder terminals first, then check the sensor, wiring and range setting before you suspect the pen drive or the servo amplifier.

Which is better for a new plant, paper or paperless recorder?

For most new plants a paperless recorder is the better choice, because it stores many channels electronically and exports data to a PC or SCADA. A paper strip chart recorder still makes sense as a like for like replacement or where a simple signed chart is required.

What We Learn Today

  • A strip chart recorder moves a pen across the chart in proportion to the signal while the paper moves at a fixed speed in mm/h.
  • Time per division equals division size divided by chart speed, so 5 mm at 20 mm/h gives 15 minutes and a 25 m roll lasts 1250 hours.
  • Most trace faults come from the input loop, earthing, pen or chart drive, so check them with a calibrator at 0, 50 and 100 percent.
